newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end sharply lower on Nov output jump.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end sharply lower on Nov output jump.

text.p: U.S. Treasury price finished sharply lower on Monday, hurt by a jump in November industrial production and buffeted by higher energy prices, an intra-day reversal in the stock market and a slumping dollar.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended at 98-11/32, down 21/32, its yield at 6.63 percent versus 6.58 percent at Friday's close.
The market opened higher after it was bid up overseas in Tokyo and London.
Some of that strength dissipated in early New York trade.

Then, when the Federal Reserve reported that industrial production had risen 0.9 percent in November, the biggest rise in nine months and a stronger figure than the market had anticipated, bond prices went into negative territory.
"The industrial production report caused some disappointment, though it was not as strong as the initial headline implied," said Marilyn Schaja, senior economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette.
The Fed tied about half the increase in November output to a rebound in motor vehicle and auto part production.
The rebound was due to the settlement of a strike against General Motors that crimped the carmaker's October production.

Unusually cold weather pumped up utility output, a factor that added about 0.2 percent to November industrial output, the Fed said. Capacity use, the portion of the nation's mines, factories and utilites employed in its production, rose, meanwhile, to 83.3 percent from 82.9 percent in October.
"The production figures weighed negatively on bond prices," said William Sullivan, senior vice president and director of fixed-income research at Dean Witter Reynolds.
Nikko Securities Co. chief economist Robert Brusca said the December National Association of Home Builders survey helped shove the bond market still lower in afternoon trade.

The builders said its Housing Market Index rose two points to 53 in December from 51 in November. The component index for single-family sales in the next six months rose to 63 from 58, the builders' survey said.
"Interest rates came down after mid-year and the idea that those lower rates could stimulate the economy has hurt the bond market," said Brusca.

Brusca contended that the home builders' survey made players wary of the next government report on housing starts, due on Tuesday. Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that housing starts bounced to an annualized 1.390 million in November from October's annualized 1.366 million.
Bond prices also came under pressure from a big jump in crude oil prices, a gain linked to anticipation of extremely cold weather across big sections of the United States.
"The energy markets went ballistic today," said Sullivan. "That had a mildly negative influence on bond prices."

The short end of the market did not appear to benefit from an intra-day stock market reversal that could have spurred some flight-to-quality buying. The Dow Jones industrial average ended down more than 36 points after being up just over 50 points during the session.
"A weak equity market in late 1996 is not going to rescue bonds," said Sullivan.
Three-month Treasury bill rates ended five basis points higher at 4.85 percent. Six-month bill rates rose three basis points to 5.02 percent. Year bill rates rose four basis points to 5.19 percent.
Two-year notes fell 3/32 to 99-21/32, yielding 5.81 percent.
Five-year notes dropped 8/32 to 98-31/32, yielding 6.12 percent.
Ten-year notes slid 13/32 to 100-29/32 to end with a 6.37 percent yield.
-- North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1679
